youtube.title: Why GoPro Karma Drone Failed So Fast: The 16-Day Recall
youtube.description:
The GoPro Karma drone launched in October 2016 and was recalled just sixteen days later because it could lose power mid-flight. Why did GoPro build a drone at all, and what happened to GoPro's drone business? This documentary follows the filings, the recall notice and the loose battery latch to find out why the Karma failed so fast.

This documentary follows the filings, the recall notice and GoPro's own statements: the camera boom, the rival that started making its own cameras, the delay, the eight days that put DJI's Mavic Pro ahead, the loose battery latch, and the job cuts that followed until GoPro left the drone business in January 2018.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: If you'd run GoPro in 2015, would you have built a drone or stayed the camera on everyone else's? 👇

sources.claim: In January 2018 GoPro said it would stop making drones, fifteen months after Karma went on sale
sources.source: GoPro press release, 8 January 2018; Karma on sale 23 October 2016 per GoPro launch release, 19 September 2016

sources.claim: GoPro shares closed near $94 in October 2014 ($93.85 closing high)
By January 2018 the shares traded below a tenth of the 2014 peak
Karma went on sale on 23 October 2016 at $799 without a camera, $1,099 with a Hero5 Black
On 8 November 2016, 16 days after launch, GoPro recalled all roughly 2,500 Karma drones sold because they could lose power during operation, with full refunds and no injuries reported
sources.source: GoPro press release, 8 November 2016; US Consumer Product Safety Commission recall notice, November 2016

sources.claim: GoPro began in 2002 with a California surfer who wanted close-up footage from the water
sources.source: GoPro Form S-1 registration statement, May 2014

sources.claim: The first product, sold in 2004, was a wrist strap with a 35mm film camera
GoPro listed on the Nasdaq in June 2014 at $24 a share, raising about $427 million
sources.source: GoPro IPO pricing release, 25 June 2014; Form 424B4 prospectus, June 2014

sources.claim: GoPro was valued at more than $11 billion at its October 2014 peak
sources.source: Nasdaq prices x shares outstanding, GoPro 10-Q Q3 2014; reported by Bloomberg, October 2014

sources.claim: 2014 revenue $1.39 billion, net profit $128 million
GoPro's YouTube channel used customer footage as marketing
DJI was founded in 2006 in Shenzhen
sources.source: DJI corporate history; Forbes profile of DJI, May 2015

sources.claim: DJI's Phantom, launched January 2013, carried a GoPro camera
In October 2013 DJI released a Phantom with its own built-in camera
GoPro shipped 6.6 million cameras in 2015; revenue $1.62 billion
2015 net profit fell to $36 million from $128 million
Hero4 Session launched at $399 in July 2015, cut to $299 within two months and $199 by December
sources.source: GoPro product announcements July, September and December 2015; GoPro Q3 2015 results, October 2015

sources.claim: GoPro ran a media division to sell its footage as entertainment, closed 30 November 2016
sources.source: GoPro Form 10-K for 2015; GoPro restructuring release, 30 November 2016

sources.claim: At the Code Conference in May 2015 the founder said GoPro's drone would arrive in the first half of 2016
sources.source: Code Conference interview, 27 May 2015, reported by Recode

sources.claim: Forbes reported partnership talks between GoPro and DJI had broken down in 2014
DJI shipped the Phantom 3 in April 2015 and the Phantom 4 in March 2016 at $1,399, with obstacle sensing
sources.source: DJI launch announcements, 8 April 2015 and 1 March 2016

sources.claim: In May 2016 GoPro delayed Karma to the holiday season
sources.source: GoPro Q1 2016 results and earnings call, 5 May 2016

sources.claim: Q1 2016 revenue $183.5 million, down almost half (49%) year on year
Karma was unveiled with the Hero5 cameras at Squaw Valley, California, on 19 September 2016; it folded into a backpack and had a detachable Karma Grip
DJI unveiled the Mavic Pro on 27 September 2016 at $999 with a built-in 4K camera, 27-minute flight time, 7 km range and forward obstacle sensing
Karma: 20-minute flight time, 1 km range, no obstacle avoidance
The Karma Grip stayed on sale during the recall
On 3 November 2016 GoPro cut its 2016 revenue forecast to $1.25-1.30 billion, citing production delays
On 30 November 2016 GoPro announced about 200 job cuts (about 15%), closed its entertainment division and said its president would leave at year end
2016 revenue $1.185 billion, net loss $419 million
In February 2017 GoPro said the cause was a battery latch that could come loose, and put Karma back on sale
sources.source: GoPro statement on Karma's return, February 2017, reported by The Verge

sources.claim: In March 2017 GoPro cut another 270 jobs
On 8 January 2018 GoPro said it would sell remaining Karma inventory and exit drones; Karma was the No. 2 best-selling drone in its price band in 2017
'the margins are unsustainable in an extremely competitive aerial market'
'a hostile regulatory environment in Europe and the United States will likely reduce the total addressable market in the years ahead'
More than 250 job cuts and the founder's 2018 cash pay cut to $1
More than 700 job cuts in about fourteen months (about 200 + 270 + more than 250)
2017 net loss $183 million
DJI launched the Osmo Action camera in May 2019
GoPro had more than two million paying subscribers by the end of 2021
Cloud computing (AWS) is Amazon's most profitable business
